title: Nirmal Purja: How a generation of record-setting guides died in a disaster which klled a climbing legend
description: Purja, 43, also known as Nims, was the leading figure of the 10-member international team up Broad Peak, the world's 12th highest mountain, when the a
body: Purja, 43, also known as Nims, was the leading figure of the 10-member international team up Broad Peak, the world's 12th highest mountain, when the avalanche struck."Nims of course was iconic and undisputedly amongst the best of his generation," says Ben Ayers, a longtime Everest reporter for Outside Magazine.Kili Pemba Sherpa and Pur Bahadur Gurung, who were also guiding the Broad Peak expedition, were "strong climbers with a solid resume", Ayers said.Kili Pemba, 46, had just earned the coveted mountaineering Grand Slam after completing his last of the 14 highest peaks, also known as eight-thousanders, in early July.Even before this crowning achievement, he was already among the best in the industry having been part of the Nepali team, led again by Purja, that completed the first winter ascent of K2 in January 2021.At the time, K2, the world's second highest peak, was the only one of the eight-thousanders not yet climbed in winter. But at 8,611m, K2 is known to be steeper, more unpredictable and deadlier than Everest (8,849m).Many have described Kili Pemba as humble and deeply committed in serving his clients. Two of the 15 times he summited Everest he did so guiding double-leg amputees up the mountain. "That was the toughest task for any guide, [Kili Pemba] did that with a lot of care," says Gyanendra Shrestha, a government official who was at Base Camp during one of these climbs.Pur Bahadur Gurung, 37, scaled 12 of the 14 highest peaks and was one of only 100 Nepali guides certified by the International Federation of Mountain Guides Association (IFMGA)."It takes a lot of money, passion and dedication to become an IFMGA guide. This tells us a lot about Pur Bahadur's zeal for mountaineering," says Himal Gautam, a spokesman for Nepal's tourism department. "It also speaks to the unprecedented loss we have suffered on Broad Peak," he adds.In 2024, Pur Bahadur was part of the team that discovered a century-old boot on Everest, believed to be that of British climber Andrew Irvine, who vanished on the mountain in 1924.The other three Nepali guides who perished on Broad Peak last week include Gyaljen Sherpa, best known for scaling the third-highest mountain Kanchenjunga three times in one season – a feat that some colleagues say deserves a Guinness World Record.Then there's Nima Sherpa, 36, who scaled four eight-thousanders in 2026 alone, and Nawang Thindu Sherpa, who in his 20s was among Nepal's rising generation of mountain guides.Nepal's mountain guides spend each spring leading international clients up Nepal's highest mountains as guides or porters. When the monsoon comes around from June to September, some of them head towards Pakistan's far north, home to some of the world's highest peaks, including five eight-thousanders. International visitors to this rugged region are relatively few, but demand is growing. While over a million adventure travellers go to the Himalayas each year, the Karakoram mountains in Pakistan attract only about 15,000 hikers annually.Some credit Purja for bringing Pakistan onto the radar of mountaineers through his feat of scaling the 14 peaks in just over six months, which was documented in a Netflix film."Nims' success gave many [guides] and foreigners the courage to believe that this mountaineering crown was truly possible," says Iswari Paudel, acting president of the Nepal Mountaineering Association."This has made Pakistan a major overseas base for Nepali Sherpas. And while helping foreign climbers fulfil their dreams, many guides have themselves completed the 14 peaks," Iswari says.Ayers, the Everest reporter, says Purja helped "publicise a new era of mountaineering" which in many ways helped "democratise mountain-climbing", but also "fuelled commercialisation and risk".Because of how remote Pakistan's mountains are, it is far more challenging to organise expeditions there – a feat that only the best guides undertake, Sherpas tell the BBC."We have to fix our own ropes, cut our steps into the ice, and set up camps as we go along," says Nima Rinji Sherpa. The 20-year-old set a new record in 2024 as the youngest mountaineer to summit the world's 14 highest peaks."Even in an era of commercial mountaineering, we experience real, old-fashioned mountaineering [in Pakistan]," he says.But because the region is hard to access, climbers usually attempt two to three mountains per trip, which makes the itinerary very tight, Nima Rinji adds.In Nepal, by contrast, mountaineering infrastructure is well-developed. The main trekking routes towards Everest are lined with family-run lodges that offer beds, hot meals and other facilities.Emergency evacuations are also generally easier in the Himalayas, where there is an integrated network of rescue helicopters and aid outposts at high altitude, whereas the Karakoram range, being more isolated, features fewer accessible landing zones."In the Pakistan mountains, getting the helicopters to base camp already takes a lot more effort, let alone flying them above high camps. "Therefore, the Sherpas who are capable of working in high-pressure situations, and who have diverse experiences and multiple skills are the ones who will operate in Pakistan," Nima Rinji says.While the Broad Peak disaster may spur calls to tighten safety standards, many believe it will do little to change high-altitude tourism."Generally, these tragedies cause a moment of concern... but then things go back to how they were. It's difficult to say with any conviction that any accident in the mountains is 'preventable' as the inherent danger is so high... and that's part of the appeal," Ayers says.The mountaineering community is drawn to high-risk pursuits, says Medhavi Gulati, a researcher specialising in high-altitude mountaineering."Often, it's the dangers and risk of death that attracts people," she says.The existing generation of mountain guides will continue to crave the global fame and world records that their predecessors have attained, she says. "I don't think that appeal will ever go away," she says."We've seen disasters like this one before, and nothing changed," says expert mountaineer and writer Alan Arnette, who pointed to how an ice avalanche on Everest killed 16 Sherpas in April 2014, and the 11 climbers who died on K2 in 2008 after a massive chunk of ice broke off."I doubt the Broad Peak incident will have a significant impact, given history. I hope I'm wrong," he says.

schema.headline: Nirmal Purja: How a generation of record-setting guides died in a disaster which klled a climbing legend

title: How to avoid the worst of the Italian heatwave this summer
description: Image source, ReutersByMalu CursinoTemperatures across Italy are soaring to levels deemed threatening to people's health and wellbeing. Looking ahead
body: Image source, ReutersByMalu CursinoTemperatures across Italy are soaring to levels deemed threatening to people's health and wellbeing. Looking ahead to Thursday, the ministry of health has issued a red alert for all of Italy's 27 major cities, external, including popular tourist destinations Milan, Naples, Venice and Rome.As Europe's holiday season continues, the BBC spoke to experts about how to make the most of Italy during this latest heatwave.While some Italians say the current heat is "not a new phenomenon" given climate change, others from southern Italy have voiced their shock when visiting northern cities and towns.Time your outingsVisiting outdoor attractions during Italy's hottest hours (after lunchtime) is a "big mistake", Simone Quilici, director of the Archaeological Park of the Colosseum, tells the BBC.The Colosseum is not prescriptive about when people should visit, instead directing visitors to guidance from the regional authorities.To make visits cooler, the ministries of tourism and culture are allowing some attractions to stay open into the evening.Last week the government shared these additional opening hours, external during August:Colosseum (Rome) - open Fridays and Saturdays between 19:45 to 23:30Pantheon (Rome) - open from 19:00 to 23:00 every day except ThursdaysSforza Castle (Milan) - open from 17:30 until 19:30Image source, ReutersIn the Colosseum, cooling fans with mists have been set up in the entrances. Staff have also increased the number of medical stations available for emergencies. While temperatures are high, Rome has become used to it, Quilici says, explaining this is not an isolated situation but the "global phenomenon" of climate change.In his role as director of the Archaeological Park of the Colosseum, Quilici says he is in talks with archaeologists to introduce more shade-providing vegetation.Also in Rome, Mateo Medina says his team have introduced tours from 22:00 until midnight. Medina, director of operations at Vivicos International Travel, has also seen higher demand for 08:00 tours.Seek out parks, museums and churchesAir conditioned museums are unsurprisingly top of the heat-escaping list. Visiting some of Italy's many churches is another way to shelter from the heat, while absorbing the Catholic nation's heritage.Cooking classes and wine tasting sessions - usually hosted in venues with air conditioning - are becoming a popular alternative to walking tours, Medina says.He also recommends the capital's parks - villa Borghese, villa Adriana, Parque de Acquedotti - for shade, and visiting the underground Catacombs of San Sebastian and San Callisto.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Locals and tour guides who spoke to the BBC recommend sheltering from the sun during Italy's hottest hoursMarco Carrino, a tour guide in Naples, warns against visiting open archaeological sites during the hottest hours of the day. Many of his tours are to Pompeii. He recommends getting up early or, if possible, avoiding the hotter months altogether. He also encourages tourists to head to the National Archaeological Museum of Naples, which he says is "very important for archaeology and has a great Roman, Egyptian and even Greek collection".For Italian travel expert and writer Alessia Armenise, supermarkets are an underrated gem. As well as being air conditioned, she says you can do what she does and head to their deli counters and grab a reasonably priced, fresh and made-to-order sandwich "instead of queuing for those silly focaccia places that honestly taste the exact same". Go off the beaten track, and book aheadImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Enjoying a Sicilian granita - or Rome's grattachecca - is another way to stay coolIf you are somewhere in Italy with a natural body of water, or any water feature, plan your activities around it, Armenise says."Instead of walking, get a boat," she says. "Sometimes you will see things you cannot access via land."Instead of hiking a coastline, you can see it from the sea, she explains, with the added bonus of cooling water splashing on you.For Dr Agata Chrzanowksa, an art historian and tour guide in Florence, the hills and mountains north of the city are "a very good spot to runaway from the heat" for those driving. She highlights the Garfagnana region in particular.If seeing attractions like the Vatican in Rome is a non-negotiable, Armenise suggests booking in advance to avoid waiting in line in scorching temperatures.Several landmarks sell tickets online ahead of time. However, you need to be organised as tickets tend to sell out quickly, Medina says.Do as locals doWhile world-renowned attractions like the Colosseum might be top of your list, it's worth trying out local galleries and museums in smaller towns and cities which will often be less crowded and have a cafe where you can stay for hours, Armenise says.In a recent trip to Bologna, the travel writer felt so warm one evening that she decided to head to the cinema.While watching a film is something you could do back home, she says people might stumble on an old theatre which is "still a part of the history of that city".If you find yourself in Verona in need of an evening activity, she suggests a concert at the Verona Arena, an amphitheatre in the city centre.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, One of Florence's tour guides suggests heading to the Odeon cafe and bookstore to cool downDr Chrzanowksa, asked if she can share any local tips, suggests Florence's Odeon cafe and bookstore.She describes it as a "recently modernised art-nouveau cinema/theatre transformed into a beautiful bookshop where you can order and drink, with air con, and relax a little bit with books around you".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, As someone used to the heat, Giusto says "the best advice I can give is simply good common sense when visiting Venice in the summer"Venetian tour guide Fiona Giusto, who runs Venice Tours, plans most of her routes around shaded stopping spots. Like other tour guides, Giusto always urges tourists to stay hydrated, wear a hat and sunscreen.To get some culture without the heat, she suggests heading to Venice's Teatro La Fenice - a historic opera house - and the Ca' Rezzonico art museum. "The best advice I can give is good common sense," she adds.

schema.headline: How to avoid the worst of the Italian heatwave this summer

title: South Africa anti-immigration protests: The stories of a Nigerian and Ghanaian who left
description: I left my wife and twins behind - why this Nigerian man fled South AfricaImage source, BBC/Gift UfuomaImage caption, Richard Itoro says returning to N
body: I left my wife and twins behind - why this Nigerian man fled South AfricaImage source, BBC/Gift UfuomaImage caption, Richard Itoro says returning to Nigeria and starting again was the better optionByMakuochi OkaforBBC AfricaReporting fromLagos and Thomas NaadiBBC AfricaReporting fromAccraNigerian Richard Itoro is not sure when he will see his twin children again.Fearing for his safety as the anti-migrant protests cranked up in South Africa this year, the 47-year-old left his family and business behind in Johannesburg and boarded one of the voluntary repatriation flights to Nigeria in June.His is just one of many experiences that is fuelling diplomatic tension and threatening to rupture relations between South Africa and other countries on the continent. Tens of thousands of foreigners have left the country over the past two months."It was painful for me to leave [the] person who's my best friend," Itoro tells the BBC, with tears welling up, as he reflects on saying goodbye to his South African wife.Over 15 years, he had built up a car-dealership business, bought a home and created a family. That is now all gone for him.Itoro became the target of harassment but his wife was not spared the intimidation. He says his neighbours told her: "You're married to a Nigerian. Those of you who are married to Nigerians we are supposed to arrest you people."You guys betrayed us. Go and leave the country with your husband and don't be here."Itoro was baffled."My family was just a small family, which was beautiful and peaceful. I had no issues with anybody."The pressure became too much."If I go home and start all over again, it's better than being here, being harassed, being scared for my life," Itoro says.Image source, Gallo Images via Getty ImagesImage caption, Marches calling for undocumented migrants to leave reached a crescendo at the end of JuneBut, the businessman says, the Nigerian high commission would not let his wife and children travel with him.He describes how leaving felt like a movie where someone boards the last helicopter flight out of a besieged city."I wish I could have just begged the people from the embassy and said: 'This is my wife, I can't leave her behind and my kids,' but I couldn't."So my car started departing and I wished I had told her not to cry."The anti-migrant groups in South Africa said their protests were aimed at undocumented foreigners. The country's outspoken Culture Minister, Gayton McKenzie, who leads one of the parties in the coalition government, also emphasised this point."We say South Africa is open to our brothers on the continent but come here legitimately. Come with your papers," he told the BBC's Interview programme.But Itoro says his legal status did not protect him from hostility as he shows the BBC a copy of the document that he says proves he had the right to stay in the country.He was not alone, according to the Nigerian authorities."We have records of Nigerians who have legitimate papers to remain in South Africa, yet they have been attacked," Nigeria's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Sola Enikanolaiye said during a recent meeting with South Africa's Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.The temperature was raised last week following the death of a Nigerian who was killed as police were arresting him over suspected drug offences. An independent body is now investigating.Lamola maintained that South Africa deals with those who take the law into their own hands, but added that President Cyril Ramaphosa was also "very firm on South Africa's sovereign right to enforce its immigration laws".Image caption, Ghanaian Emmanuel Asamoah was working as a hairdresser in South AfricaDespite the diplomatic efforts, South Africa's reputation has been severely damaged.Not least because of images and videos circulating on social media. Not all of them were what they were purported to be, but one, involving a Ghanaian, was genuine and it sparked huge concern once it started being shared in April.When Emmanuel Asamoah left Ghana in 2023 for South Africa, he was chasing the kind of opportunity many migrants dream about.The 37-year-old hairstylist settled in Soweto, on the outskirts of Johannesburg, found work, built a life and believed he had a future in one of Africa's biggest economies.But three months ago that future suddenly felt uncertain when he was surrounded by a group of South Africans who demanded that he leave. The confrontation was captured on video."This thing of you guys moving from one country to another… is no longer working," one woman can be seen telling Asamoah."Now, we are making it very clear to you guys, we don't want you here. We want you to fix your countries."Having returned to Ghana's capital, Accra, in May, Asamoah tells the BBC that the encounter left him terrified."They came to me and started pushing me... So, they started asking questions and harassing me… they said that I should go home, that we are spoiling their country, because of us, they don't eat, we are taking their girlfriends," he says.South Africa's high jobless rate - standing at more than 30% - is seen as one of the factors fuelling the tension. It was a sentiment echoed by McKenzie."No man can feed another man's children while his children are starving. Our people are starving of jobs," he said backing calls for those who came to the country without papers to leave.Image source, Gallo Images via Getty ImagesImage caption, As well as Ghana and Nigeria, Malawi also organised transport for its citizens to leave South AfricaBut Asamoah insists he had a stamp in his passport giving him permission to stay."I was not illegal. I was legal in South Africa. That's why I told them that, they can take me to the police station so that we can go to Home Affairs and verify," he says.For Asamoah, returning home has brought an unexpected fresh start. With support from a Ghanaian businessman, he has opened a cement business and is determined to build his future."My brothers and sisters in South Africa. I'm in Ghana now. I'm fixing my country," he says.But Ghana's government remains angry at the way it sees its citizens are being viewed in South Africa.In an interview with the BBC, Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa spoke about how he saw it as going against the spirit of continental solidarity and a failure to recognise how African countries helped in the struggle against apartheid, which ended in 1994.South Africa "should be the epitome of Pan-Africanism. We talk about African integration. We talk about free movement… even if you have issues with high immigration, is this how you resolve it?", the minister asked.In Lagos, Itoro is still pining for his family."It's not easy. But we talk every day, and I'm broken. There is hope, because... my wife is going to join me very soon, as soon as God lifts me up. But it was heartbreaking, and that's how I felt: like I lost everything," he says.Additional reporting by Abayomi Adisa

schema.headline: South Africa anti-immigration protests: The stories of a Nigerian and Ghanaian who left

title: Ceuta: EU commends Spain's 'swift response' to migrant crisis
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Hundreds of migrants were pictured lined up on a beach in Ceuta to collect aid BySofia Ferreira SantosThe Eur
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Hundreds of migrants were pictured lined up on a beach in Ceuta to collect aid BySofia Ferreira SantosThe European Union has praised Spain's "swift response" to the migrant crisis in Ceuta, following a meeting of the bloc's interior ministers on Tuesday.Around 72,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory in North Africa between 30 and 31 July, Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said. He added that an estimated 70,000 have since been returned to Morocco.At least 75 people died on the Spanish side of the border, while 11 deaths were reported in Morocco.Tuesday's meeting was called after several EU members expressed concern over Spain's handling of the crisis, with Italy describing images from Ceuta as "shocking" and suspending its Schengen agreement with Spain.Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan, who chaired Tuesday's meeting, said the EU stood in solidarity with Spain and that migration required "a united European response".The meeting had been expected to draw some tension, following earlier criticism of Spain from some EU nations.On Thursday, Italy's right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said such "uncontrolled immigration" was a security threat to Europe.Italy suspended its Schengen zone agreement with Spain on free movement on Friday, but since the two countries do not share a land border, this would only apply, effectively, to flights - which appears simply to mean extra checks for passengers.The Schengen agreement eliminates border checks and now encompasses more than 450 million people and 29 countries in Europe.Figure caption, Watch: Migrants started to return to Morocco after thousands entered Spain's Ceuta on 30 JulyFinland and Denmark backed Italy's move, while Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš urged a temporary suspension of Spain's Schengen membership.Italy, along with Denmark and 20 other nations, later sent a letter expressing their concern over the Ceuta migrant crisis.In response, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he had "serious concerns" about some European governments and pointed out that Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area.While most had shown "support and solidarity", he said other European governments had chosen to attack Spain, "driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest".Speaking after the meeting on Tuesday, Grande-Marlaska said the Schengen zone had not been compromised and that he hoped Italy would lift any added controls "as soon as possible".Denmark's immigration minister Morten Bødskov said he was "very satisfied" with Spain's quick response, but added that the incident showed "it is absolutely crucial that we have control over the EU's borders".Speaking afterwards, EU commissioner Magnus Brunner said the incident had been a "test" of European resilience and border security - which he said it had successfully "passed".Brunner added that the EU had offered Spain emergency financial support to strengthen its borders and manage the crisis.It is unknown exactly what led the tens of thousands of migrants to cross from Morocco into Ceuta in a span of just a few hours last week.Brunner said it is thought that the influx was fuelled by criminal networks and social media disinformation.Ayoub, a 23-year-old administrative assistant from Casablanca in Morocco, said he decided to swim across to Ceuta after seeing the situation unfold on social media.Speaking to BBC World Service Newshour programme, he described it as "the most traumatic experience I've ever had in my life".Ayoub said he wanted to reach Europe for a better quality of life."I haven't risked my life for nothing, I want to be free, I want to pursue my studies and I want a chance in life," he said.The crossings came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla, another Spanish exclave, cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.Moroccan authorities later said that it had warned Spain the ruling would cause "a problem", but Spain rejected this claim, with a government spokeswoman saying it had no evidence or intelligence "that alerted us to the magnitude of this unprecedented event".Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, The Red Cross distributed food and other aid to the remaining migrants on MondaySpain's interior minister said he was working "firmly" with Morocco to avoid further "violations" of Spain's borders and added that any migrants still in Ceuta would be returned to Morocco as soon as possible.Images from inside Ceuta on Tuesday showed crowds of migrants gathering near the beach to receive food, water and other aid. Some held makeshift banners with the word 'asylum' written on them.Several people were also pictured sleeping on the beach and on streets across the city.Concerns have been raised over the treatment of the remaining migrants, in particular of unaccompanied minors, with local media reporting some 800 children being held in facilities across the city.Ahmed Haroun, a 29-year-old Sudanese migrant, said it had been his "dream" for years to reach Ceuta.He told the Reuters news agency that he has family waiting for him, adding: "I want to help them."He said the situation had improved over the last few days and that he was now receiving aid and support, but he still does not know whether he will be allowed to stay in Spanish territory.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Groups of migrants have been sleeping on the beach in CeutaDjibril, from Senegal, criticised the Spanish government's response, saying those who arrived in Ceuta were not there "to cause trouble"."We're not thieves," he told Spanish broadcaster RTVE."But leaving us without a response is inhumane. For five days you've left people on your territory. They're not eating, they're not showering, they're ill."Kamal, a 24-year-old from Sudan, said he had been "forced" to be in Morocco and was "trying to find somewhere where I can be protected"."Now it's very difficult and it's getting more difficult," he told Reuters news agency. "No food, nowhere to sleep, not even blankets to warm up from the cold. We live in front of the beach."Spain's interior minister said the rights of all migrants, especially those underage, were being respected during the crisis, with Spain's government allocating around 25m euros (£21.4m; $28.8m) to assist minors in Ceuta.

schema.headline: Ceuta: EU commends Spain's 'swift response' to migrant crisis

title: How AI is changing jobs in the Philippines' outsourcing industry
description: 'I feel like I dug my own grave': The workers caught in the AI transitionImage source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, The Philippines is kno
body: 'I feel like I dug my own grave': The workers caught in the AI transitionImage source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, The Philippines is known as the call centre capital of the worldBySuranjana TewariAsia Business CorrespondentReporting fromManilaFor 15 years, single mother Lisa made a living from content writing.She began writing straight out of college, freelanced for years and eventually followed a path taken by many young Filipinos: joining a multinational in the country's booming outsourcing industry.Lisa says she never felt the need to use artificial intelligence (AI) in her work."I can say that I am able to do my job, I meet deadlines. In my opinion, there is no need for [AI]," she told the BBC. Eight months into her latest role, and one month before the position was due to become permanent, she was made redundant.In the months before, Lisa says a public relations agency had been tasked with producing AI-generated material that she and her colleagues were asked to edit. She says her skills were used to train the AI on the company writing style."I feel like I dug my own grave," she says. "We were the ones who trained the artificial intelligence that replaced us."Lisa, not her real name, is one of several former outsourcing employees the BBC spoke to who asked to remain anonymous. They signed confidentiality agreements in return for severance pay, and fear that speaking publicly could hurt their chances of finding work in an industry which has a small network.Their experiences offer an insight into a question confronting emerging economies like the Philippines: what happens when AI begins to automate the jobs that helped lift millions of people into the middle classes?Building an industryEvery evening around 5pm, streams of workers wearing company lanyards spill out of high-rise offices in the district of Cubao in Manila.It's one of several areas of the capital where multinational companies have premises – providing all sorts of outsourcing work including call centres, accounting, software development and marketing copy services for clients thousands of miles away.For over two decades, these business districts have symbolised one of the Philippines' biggest economic success stories.Beginning in the early 2000s, the country was promoted as an English-speaking alternative to India for what's called business process outsourcing (BPO).Successive governments offered tax incentives, invested in infrastructure and encouraged multinational companies to set up large operations.Global groups like Accenture, Concentrix and Teleperformance built sprawling campuses, employing hundreds of thousands of Filipinos.Today, the outsourcing industry employs roughly 1.9 million people, and generates $40bn (£30.1bn) in revenues every year, accounting for about 10% of the Philippines' economy.But experts say the industry is disproportionately vulnerable to the impact of AI.Image caption, The outsourcing industry employs about 1.9 million people in the PhilippinesThe International Labour Organization estimates that 12.7 million Filipinos - more than one in four workers - are employed in occupations exposed to generative AI, the highest share in South East Asia.The organisation expects many roles to change rather than disappear but the types of service jobs that people do in the Philippines leaves it particularly at risk.Jack Madrid, president of the IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines (IBPAP), admits that AI is being adopted by the sector. More than two-thirds of IBPAP's members are already running AI pilots, he says."Agentic AI has the potential to automate at a much more accelerated pace," Madrid says. "Obviously, there's a layer of jobs that are automatable or have been automated."But he adds that the vast majority of affected workers have been redeployed within the same organisations.Madrid says any weakness in hiring reflects more than the impact of AI."We've seen a slowdown in investment decisions on whether certain job functions or processes should be offshored," he says, pointing to slower global demand and uncertainty over how companies will ultimately deploy the technology.Even so, he acknowledges the challenge. "We cannot do enough to be prepared," he says. "The importance of reskilling" cannot be overstated.The pressure to automateMary, another former content writer whose name we've changed, says her employer encouraged the use of AI as a productivity tool.Instead of making her job easier, she says it created additional responsibilities."We had to edit more, fact-check more because the data AI produced was inaccurate," she says. "Technically it was more work for us."Like Lisa, she was later made redundant.Companies are under pressure to implement AI, to reduce costs and increase productivity, experts say. Teleperformance, the world's largest call centre operator and one of the Philippines' biggest private employers, has said AI offers an opportunity to augment rather than replace its workforce.The company expects AI to handle routine interactions while human agents move into more complex roles. Teleperformance has also said it plans to retrain employees.Accenture has similarly said that generative AI will reshape almost every job rather than eliminate positions.The firm has promised to invest billions of dollars in AI capabilities and workforce training.Concentrix - which is the biggest outsourcing firm in the Philippines - says its AI systems should remain under human oversight and has committed to training employees in the new technology.Some Filipino managers are uneasy about AI and want to slow down adoption, according to Paul Quintos, from the University of the Philippines-Diliman. They are concerned about how much of the domestic workforce might be displaced."But there's tremendous pressure from foreign clients to adopt AI," he says. "It's a major cost-cutting measure."Philippine outsourcing companies compete directly with rivals in India and elsewhere for contracts from multinational corporations.Increasingly, those clients expect suppliers not only to provide cheaper labour, but also to integrate AI into the services they deliver.Image caption, The BBC spoke to employees who say they trained AI before being let goDespite hundreds of billions of dollars being invested globally in AI, Quintos says there is still limited evidence about how much productivity many workplace tools actually deliver."There is a term called 'AI washing'," he says.Some layoffs are presented as being driven by AI when companies are in fact responding to weaker demand or slowing economic conditions, Quintos says.Attributing redundancies to AI, he adds, can make restructuring appear like technological progress rather than a response to market conditions.The next transitionLabour groups have told the BBC that existing employment laws in the Philippines govern redundancy but offer little guidance on how companies should introduce AI into workplaces or consult employees over its use.The Philippines' outsourcing sector is also non-unionised, leaving many workers with little formal say over how new technologies are deployed.The government says that it, and the private sector have a responsibility to retrain workers, and risks falling behind competitors like India and Singapore. "To be completely honest, I think we're slightly behind. We have to catch up," says Leandro Aguirre of the Philippines Department of Information and Communications Technology."We have to double our efforts to put our people in a position where they will not be displaced but actually thrive in this growing AI race."The government has committed to upskilling more than 300,000 outsourcing workers, but Aguirre acknowledges that the Philippines may need to rethink the economic model that helped make it an outsourcing centre."We relied heavily on foreign direct investment," he says. "But I think we also need to focus on local talent and local companies."The ambition, he says, is to build home-grown AI companies capable of creating higher-value jobs.Aguirre rejects calls for sweeping new AI legislation, arguing that existing labour, privacy and consumer protection laws can be adapted more quickly through regulatory guidance."The benefits of AI have to trickle down to people," he says. "It can't just benefit employers."For more than 20 years, the Philippines built one of the world's most successful outsourcing industries by selling the skills of its people to multinational companies.AI may not end that model, but it is certainly changing it, and risks leaving some workers behind.Additional reporting by Jaltson Akkanath Chummar and Regine Cabato

schema.headline: How AI is changing jobs in the Philippines' outsourcing industry

title: Trump challenged with cold reality by allies Todd Blanche and Jeanine Pirro
description: It's been a humbling few days for Donald Trump, even if the American president is reluctant to acknowledge it.In a series of setbacks, Trump has faced
body: It's been a humbling few days for Donald Trump, even if the American president is reluctant to acknowledge it.In a series of setbacks, Trump has faced adversity in matters both large and small; two of which he cares about dearly and one that could determine his and his party's political fate for the remaining two years of his presidential term.From a flawed attempt to renovate a Washington landmark to questions about his pick to head the justice department to increasingly complicated efforts to end his war in Iran, the president has been handling tricky issues - many of his own making. Trump's response has been a familiar one. A first term refrain - that the president makes his own reality with "alternative facts" - is still the operative one. He sticks to beliefs even in the face of conflicting evidence.Unlike his first term, however, when many of his most notable conflicts were with dissenters in his own administration, this time around he has butted heads even with those who have proven themselves the most loyal to him.On Friday, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro, a former Fox News host and stalwart Trump ally, moved to drop felony destruction of property charges against former Olympian David Hearn, who federal prosecutors had accused of intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool near the Washington Monument."The damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism," she wrote in a 20-page court filing announcing her department's decision. She attributed her decision to prosecute Hearn as the result of misleading information provided by the Department of Interior.Trump may embrace alternative facts, but the evidence Pirro confronted - what she would have had to defend in court, before a judge and potentially sceptical jury - provided scarce support for her case. And so she abandoned it.Trump had enthusiastically endorsed the vandalism explanation, however, and he stuck by it. In a Truth Social post on Saturday, he criticised Pirro's decision to drop the case and did so again in comments from the Oval Office on Monday."She folded like an umbrella," he griped.If the Reflecting Pool case was an instance of Trump being forced to face legal reality, up on Capitol Hill it was an unpleasant political reality that confronted him.One of Trump's closest allies – his former criminal defence attorney Todd Blanche – was hitting stiff headwinds in his bid to become attorney general on a permanent basis.Two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, had joined Democrats to block Blanche's nomination.  They were demanding Blanche provide a letter formally disavowing any attempts to revive the proposed $1.8bn (£1.34bn) fund to pay individuals who claimed to have been the targets of politicised government prosecution.Tillis called it a "payout pot for punks" amid concerns it could be used to compensate people prosecuted over the US Capitol riot by Trump's supporters in 2021.In another Saturday Truth Social post, Trump wrote that he would keep Blanche on as acting attorney general and "push hard" to get Congress to pass legislation authorising the fund."It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," he wrote, suggesting that no matter what the ultimate outcome of Blanche's nomination, Trump is unlikely to ever let the issue go.The political maths in the Senate, however, was undeniable. By the next day Blanche had acceded to the senators' request, releasing two letters that Tillis and Cornyn said satisfied their concerns.In comments from the White House on Monday, Blanche escaped the scolding that Pirro the prosecutor received. Trump said he "didn't look at" Blanche's documents. "I understand there's been a sign-off, but I don't know what they agreed," he said.While the Reflecting Pool prosecution and the so-called "anti-weaponisation fund" may be topics of intense presidential interest, they barely register as concerns for the larger American public.That is decidedly not the case with the war with Iran, where Trump is once again accusing Iran of deceit amid another round of on-again, off-again negotiations and threats of overwhelming American military action.On Monday, after asserting the previous day that he had called off "an attack that would have been the biggest attack since World War II" at the behest of Iranian officials and Arab intermediaries, Trump took to Truth Social to condemn what he said was Iranian duplicity after Iran denied any new direct negotiations."They ask for a meeting, some would say 'beg', talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they're not having any discussions," Trump wrote.If Iranians are misrepresenting the status of talks it wouldn't be the first time - but it also wouldn't be the first time Trump has seemingly taken their assurances at face value and heralded a new diplomatic breakthrough.US officials told the BBC's partner CBS News on Monday that no "new" or novel negotiations with Iran were planned. An Iranian official said the country's only current talks were with Oman, over the future of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.The latest twists in the war have become a familiar pattern with little progress, as polls continue to show American disapproval of the conflict and concern that Trump is not achieving his war goals.Those recent public-opinion surveys suggest the war has become a growing drag on the president's overall popularity. A recent Associated Press poll puts Trump's approval at 33%, aligned with similar findings by CNN, Quinnipiac and YouGov. That matches or is below Trump's ratings after the Capitol riot and is above only Richard Nixon – who resigned from office in disgrace - among second-term US presidents in modern American history.Trump, however, has repeatedly dismissed surveys suggesting his historic unpopularity."My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been," he posted to Truth Social on Monday.In three months, voters will head to the polls for congressional midterm elections. And Trump has shown surprising strength at the ballot box in the past, even in the face of seemingly daunting poll numbers.While Trump may be grappling with – and, at times denying - recent adversity, that will be the ultimate measure of his political fate. And if Republicans struggle, it may provide yet another reality that Trump, despite his best efforts, must eventually face.

schema.headline: Trump challenged with cold reality by allies Todd Blanche and Jeanine Pirro

title: Kenya elephant deaths: Behind the poisoning and the pesticide mystery
description: Mysterious elephant deaths in Kenya raise questions around pesticides Image source, Getty ImagesByThomas MukhwanaAfrica correspondentReporting fromAmb
body: Mysterious elephant deaths in Kenya raise questions around pesticides Image source, Getty ImagesByThomas MukhwanaAfrica correspondentReporting fromAmboseliUpdated 2 hours agoNews that the recent deaths of 15 elephants may have been caused by pesticides sprayed on tomato crops surrounding Amboseli National Park has raised concerns and questions in Kenya.Last week, the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) said that some of the elephants that had died between 24 June and 24 July had shown signs of "partial paralysis" that pointed to poisoning from cyanide used in pesticides.But conservationists have told the BBC that, perhaps, is not the full story. Farmers we have spoken to in the area were also sceptical."We have stayed with this wildlife for decades and have never experienced this," Daniel Nina, who represents some of the landowners in the area, told the BBC."So that's why we are wondering why it is happening today."The tomato farms are found in the Kimana area, which is part of a corridor between Amboseli National Park and the Tsavo National Park in the south of Kenya.It is a vast area known as the Amboseli ecosystem, which straddles the border near Tanzania where more than 2,000 elephants move along in search of food and water.These farms thrive thanks to the streams from nearby Mount Kilimanjaro and supply markets in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, and beyond.Image caption, The 15 elephants were found dead outside the Amboseli National Park between June and JulyThe chief vet of Kenya's Wildlife Service, Dr Isaac Lekolool, told us that they had found traces of cyanide in samples taken from the elephants' stomachs.He says that they are not ruling out deliberate poisoning but it's impossible at this stage to tell what could have killed the elephants."It's difficult to tell because we've not seen these kind of cases before. It is almost like a one-off, and it was within a period of about a month," Lekolool said.Their working theory is that the elephants were exposed to the toxin through pesticides sprayed on nearby tomato farms."It could be unintentional. Maybe people are trying to do some controls of pests on their crops, and that could have been maybe a source."Pesticide problemA 2024 report by Kenyan food safety initiative Route to Food found a farmer in Kimana area using an insecticide that had an "active ingredient" that was "a chemical compound of cyanide". Wangunyu Njuguna, the author of the report, said that despite being illegal in Kenya, some toxic agrochemicals are smuggled through the border with Tanzania."The biggest problem is we're not enforcing similar standards in the region," Njuguna said. "There is no-one checking what I go and buy across the border, so I can just go buy anything and walk through the border and no-one stops me."Highly hazardous substances are common on Kenyan farms and some have been linked to serious diseases. While regulations against illegal agrochemicals exist, there's weak enforcement and little attention paid to how they can affect animals.Image source, Peter Njoroge/BBCImage caption, Officials suggest that pesticides sprayed on tomatoes in nearby farms could have poisoned the elephants'It's not adding up'However, we have spoken to several wildlife conservationists who have questioned the initial findings of Kenya's Wildlife Service. Paula Kahumbu is a world-renowned conservationist who has worked with elephants for nearly 30 years. "We haven't got enough detailed information to have confidence in this claim that it's due to pesticides in crops," Kahumbu said."Some information has been released to the public but it's not adding up. Those elephants have to eat a huge amount to kill them."Other experts who did not want to be named said the pesticide theory was inconsistent with elephant behaviour. They said that males are more likely to raid farms as they usually take more risks than females and calves. However, only one of the 15 elephants affected was an adult male.Nina, the landowners' representative, added that unlike the latest incident, previous cases of poisoning in farms had affected zebras and antelopes, which raid the same areas. "How does cyanide kill the elephants and leave behind the zebras, antelopes and wildebeests, which are eating the grass together?" Nina asked.Human-wildlife conflict has persisted for decades in communities near conservation areas across Kenya.Stephen Michael, a tomato farmer in Kimana, says elephants and giraffes occasionally raid farms in the area. "Elephants come from time to time from Tsavo and Amboseli. They destroy many farms, not just mine," Michael said."The last time elephants came, they destroyed cabbages and tomatoes. I lost cabbages worth almost $1,535. That doesn't include tomatoes. I might start crying if I count that."Frank Pope, CEO of conservation organisation Save the Elephants, told the BBC the pressure on Amboseli's elephants isn't ivory anymore."It's land use," he said.Farms and lodges are increasingly taking up land around the park which was previously used by elephants. It is such activities that Pope says worsen the conflict with wildlife."People are moving into areas where there's enough water to grow crops, and fertile soils, and those are the very areas that the elephants tend to use as well."Nobody knows for sure what's causing the elephant deaths now. The fear is that the remaining elephants and the people who live near them could still be at risk.

schema.headline: Kenya elephant deaths: Behind the poisoning and the pesticide mystery

title: India CJP protests: Young women face online harassment and abuse
description: 'I was slut-shamed' - Indian women 'cockroach' protesters doxxed and abusedImage source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, The women BBC
body: 'I was slut-shamed' - Indian women 'cockroach' protesters doxxed and abusedImage source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, The women BBC spoke to say they received threats and abuses after participating in  the CJP protestsByZoya Mateen and Nikita YadavBBC News, DelhiTheir videos lasted only a few seconds: lip-syncs, sarcastic reels and jokes filmed on the way to protests.But while thousands of young people filled social media with memes and videos mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi during one of India's biggest anti-government protest in years, many of the women behind those posts say they have paid a heavy price for speaking out.The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led movement that helped force the resignation of India's education minister, relied as much on Instagram as it did on marches. Memes, reels and viral videos became the movement's calling card, documenting everything from protest songs to the police crackdown when officers used tear gas and baton charges to stop demonstrators marching to parliament on 20 July. Delhi police said 60 protesters and 118 police personnel were injured on the day, but the CJP said the number of injured protesters was significantly higher than the official count.The posts reached hundreds of thousands of people, turning ordinary students into some of the movement's most recognisable faces.Since the protests ended, police have opened criminal cases against some protesters. But many women say another reckoning played out online. They describe rape threats, doctored images spreading on social media and strangers trawling through their photos and videos. Some cases spilled into TV debates, police complaints and political statements. Many more unfolded quietly, as young women deleted posts, locked their accounts and stopped answering calls from unknown numbers.The BBC spoke to four women and reviewed screenshots of abusive messages, posts and other material they shared. Their names have not been used to protect their identities.Content creatorI'm in my mid-20s. I had been posting about the protests from the beginning, but 20 July was the first time I attended one.After the baton charge that day and the internet shutdown around the protest site, I went home and started sharing first-person accounts on Instagram. I also helped organise food, aid and volunteers. I thought I was just helping and didn't think of it as political.But the hate started almost immediately.I was slut-shamed and I was attacked for questioning the prime minister's comments, external after the protest ended. [Modi said he forgave the children who had abused him, urging society to do the same rather than punish them or drag them through the courts.] I have lost count of the number of messages I have deleted and people I have blocked. But the comments keep coming.As a content creator, I already live with this feeling of constantly being watched. Every word I say is scrutinised, mostly by men.When I first started creating content, I would block men if they made me feel uncomfortable. Over time, the algorithm started pushing my content towards more women. I believe that has shielded me from abuse compared with many other female creators.And still, this happened.My mother stopped reading the comments on my posts long ago. She said she couldn't bear the things strangers were saying about her daughter. I understood. What parent wouldn't be frightened by that?As a woman in India, you grow up with fear. You're told not to stay out late, to watch where you go, who you're with and how you'll get home. You learn early that your safety is something you must constantly think about.When you have a voice online, that fear doesn't disappear. It just follows you there.Image source, EPAImage caption, Police used tear gas and baton charge to disperse protesters who tried to march to the parliament on 20 JulyCollege studentI am 20 years old, and this was my first protest. I went because I believed the students were standing up for something important. Before leaving the Metro station, I propped my phone against a railing and filmed a quick "fit check" [a video showing off her outfit before the protest.] "Going to get beaten by cops, guys," I joked. That's the kind of light-hearted videos I usually make.When police fired tear gas and charged protesters that afternoon, I kept filming. I was simply recording what was happening around me, as I always do. I never imagined those videos would reach far beyond my followers.I was wrong.One of them was shown on a national TV channel. Soon afterwards, my face began appearing in social media posts claiming protesters were being identified by the police. Someone even found out which college I attended. That's when I realised people weren't just attacking me online. They were trying to find me.My inbox filled with anonymous messages. Some said they would report me to the police so I would be beaten or arrested. Men called me degrading names associated with prostitution, made sexually explicit remarks, mocked my body and threatened violence. Some said I should be "taught a lesson". Others simply warned: "Your turn will come."What frightened me most wasn't the abuse itself, but what followed. Relatives and acquaintances called my parents, urging them to make me delete my videos or face the consequences. Seeing them so frightened was devastating. That's why I don't want my name published. I've since removed or archived almost all my protest videos.I worry less about what could happen to me than what they might do to my parents. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Several young women have faced online abuse and harassment after the protests Student activistI have always spoken my mind online. I'm a student activist and a Muslim, part of a religious minority in an increasingly polarised India. None of that ever frightened me.But after the CJP protests, everything changed.My Instagram account is private now. I've muted most of my other social media because the abuse has been unrelenting. Every time I look at my phone, there's another offensive comment or message or post about me.I went to the protest because I believed it was the right thing to do. I made a few satirical videos during the march. One mocked the prime minister. Others showed us singing on stage and chanting slogans. They were political, irreverent and the kind of videos I'd always made.But they spread far beyond the people I knew.One Instagram page edited a photograph to make it appear as though I was kissing a man to shame me. Another morphed my images and branded me an anti-national and a terrorist.I was also called a hijra - using the term for South Asia's transgender community as an insult - and dismissed as a paid protester.When my father, a journalist, read the comments, he panicked. He kept asking why I had spoken out. He said that once people saw my Muslim name, nothing else would matter. My parents have watched other Muslim activists investigated and arrested, and fear the same could happen to me.We live under constant dread. But I'm not going to stop speaking up. I still believe I was right to go to that protest. Now I just understand the cost much better than I did before.Image source, EPAImage caption, Memes and satirical short-form videos became a popular way for young protesters to speak about the movementStudentI'm a student in [the state of] West Bengal, where political discussions are an integral part of college life. I've participated in those conversations on campus for years, so I didn't think much before posting online about the protests.Although I first joined the Kolkata protest on 20 July, I'd already been helping online, organising supplies ranging from diabetic biscuits to masks for people worried about being identified. A friend and I also launched an Instagram fundraiser.But on 24 July, the police started detaining protesters in the state and we began talking about it online.That's when the hate really started. People began leaving spiteful comments on my fundraiser post; they called me a prostitute in private messages. They did not stop even after the protest had ended - and eventually I deleted the post.In the days that followed, the fear of being doxxed became real. I changed my name on social media, made my account private and blocked messages from people I didn't know.What hurt most was that none of my male friends faced the abuse I did. They expressed similar views but weren't targeted over their sexuality or subjected to insults about their mothers. I was.When it comes to women, the response quickly becomes about our gender. That's left me wondering why women can't express the same opinions as men online.

schema.headline: India CJP protests: Young women face online harassment and abuse

title: Armed man arrested at Trump's golf course ahead of president's visit
description: Authorities in California have arrested a man who was seen near a golf course owned by President Donald Trump in the Los Angeles area, ahead of the pr
body: Authorities in California have arrested a man who was seen near a golf course owned by President Donald Trump in the Los Angeles area, ahead of the president's visit for a fundraising dinner there. Jeanine John Taele, 38, was found with a pistol and illegal ammunition at the Trump National Golf Course in Rancho Palos Verdes, investigators say.According to the Los Angeles Sheriff's Department, he was "observed walking throughout the golf course grounds taking photographs and videos and appearing to monitor security-planning activities".The arrest took place on Sunday afternoon. Trump is currently visiting California to attend a Republican party fundraising dinner at the course on Tuesday.Taele is being held on charges of carrying a concealed firearm and possession of armour-piercing/prohibited ammunition. In a news release, the sheriff's department said Taele was arrested after plainclothes federal agents reported a suspicious person to local authorities during the middle of the day, around 1530 ET (2330 BST). When police confronted the man, they discovered that he was being sought in connection to a robbery by the El Segundo Police Department, about 15 miles (25km) north of Rancho Palos Verdes, a wealthy coastal enclave known for its hills and scenic cliffs. Authorities searched him and found he was carrying a 16-round magazine containing hollow point ammunition. In his vehicle, which was parked at the golf course, they found a loaded pistol, along with a loaded magazine containing hollow-point ammunition. Hollow point bullets flatten and widen on impact, causing maximum damage to vital organs. California, which has some of the strictest gun laws in the US, has banned magazines capable of holding more than 10 bullets. The suspect's home in Downey, a city also in the LA-area, was raided on Monday by agents from the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force and the LA County Sheriff's Department Major Crimes Bureau.The sheriff's department said his home was searched due to the "potential security implications surrounding the incident". Inside his home, they found an "illegally modified AR platform rifle" a .45 pistol, body armour, high-capacity magazines, a plethora of bullets for pistols and rifles and multiple notebooks "containing concerning statements". The investigation is continuing, with assistance from the US Secret Service, and officials say more charges may be filed later.The sheriff's statement adds that they have not identified any "credible threat to our communities"."However, this case underscores the importance of vigilance, strong partnerships with local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies, and the proactive steps taken to identify and investigate suspicious activity before it can escalate."The arrest happened during a rare visit to California by the president. He is planning to attend a Republican fundraising dinner at his golf courseAccording to the White House, Trump was due to give a speech critical of California Governor Gavin Newsom, who is widely considered to be planning a run for the presidency in the 2028 election, after Trump's second term ends.On Wednesday, Trump is travelling to Las Vegas to deliver a speech at a casino.The visits come as campaign activity ramps up ahead of the mid-term elections in November, when the balance of power in Congress is up for grabs.Trump has survived three assassination attempts in recent years. After the most recent, when a gunman stormed a hotel in Washington during a White House dinner, Trump's security team said they would review their protocols for protecting the president. Officials have not said whether the suspect in Rancho Palos Verdes was seeking to hurt Trump and he is not facing any criminal charges related to such allegations.

schema.headline: Armed man arrested at Trump's golf course ahead of president's visit

title: More than 170 migrants rescued after boat catches fire in Channel
description: More than 170 migrants have been rescued after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire on Tuesday morning, as the UK government said
body: More than 170 migrants have been rescued after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire on Tuesday morning, as the UK government said "all will be returned" to France.The boat was attempting to cross to the UK when its engine caught fire, according to the French maritime prefecture of the Channel and North Sea.It had originally reported 157 migrants were rescued, but has since revised that figure up to 173. All have been taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer in France, with 11 people suffering from minor injuries.French prosecutors have opened an investigation, and an Egyptian national has been taken into policy custody in connection with the incident.Border Security Minister Anna Turley said the incident "shows the dangers of these illegal crossings and the ruthless gangs behind them"."That's why we are bearing down on them," she said.French authorities said the boat left France on Monday night.Overnight "five people on board the vessel required rescue... the remaining people on board refused the assistance offered by the French patrol boats", the French maritime prefecture said."Determined to reach the United Kingdom, migrants crossing the Channel in small boats refused assistance offered by French emergency service, accepting it only in situations of extreme emergency," it said in a statement.Because of the "structural fragility" of boats used to cross the Channel, it said they decided not to intervene further at that stage.But this morning the engine caught fire and the "vessel's integrity deteriorated very rapidly". Rescue boats went to the scene from France and the UK, including the RNLI Eastbourne lifeboat and the UK Border Force vessels BSC Contender and BSC Courageous.The French maritime prefecture said the operation involved 40 firefighters, 13 police officers, seven interpreters, and a number of medical personnel.It had previously reported that 157 migrants were rescued, but on Tuesday afternoon revised that figure up to 173.On top of the initial five rescued, two French boats rescued 105 migrants and the British boats rescued 63. All of them were taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer for treatment.The total number on the boat broke the previous record of 165 people, who reached the UK late last month in a 42ft (13m) boat, making it the largest single vessel to attempt to cross the Channel carrying migrants.Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: "This is why it's so wrong that French police stand by and do nothing while the illegal migrant boats embark – lives are being risked."Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said in a post on X: "We must put a stop to this. Our plan will save lives."Earlier this week, his party said if in government it would deploy the navy to ward off crossings.Political discussions around the UK's policies on illegal migration have resurfaced since tens of thousands of migrants swam into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on Thursday.The Conservatives have said that Labour has not delivered on its promises on migration, while the Lib Dems said the government should increase efforts to improve relationships with Europe and cut down the asylum backlog.The number of migrants who have arrived in the UK on small boats since Burnham became prime minister a fortnight ago surpassed 2,000 on Saturday.Last Wednesday was the busiest day for crossings so far this year, with 752 migrants arriving in the UK.Most people attempt the crossing in the summer when conditions are better. It's also become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally.Home Office figures show the number of crossings so far this year are down about 43% compared to this time last year. The number peaked in 2022 and has been on a downward trend ever since.During a visit to Dover on Monday, Prime Minister Burnham pledged his government will be "relentless" in curbing the number of people arriving in the UK on small boats.He said progress had been made in curbing the number of people arriving in the UK on small boats, adding that "people want to see this issue addressed".Burnham said enforcement officers tackling people-smuggling gangs have been doubled on both sides of the Channel, but "a system that offers safe routes for people" needs to be built as well.In April, the UK and France struck a £662m (773m euro) deal aiming to stop illegal migrants from crossing the Channel.The three-year agreement included plans to send riot-trained police to French beaches to tackle violence and "hostile crowds", as well as France deploying millions of pounds of drones and two helicopters as part of a system to intercept people smugglers and illegal migrants.UK ministers have also said about £100m in funding could be redirected or withdrawn after a year if not enough journeys are stopped - but the government has not confirmed what targets the French would have to meet.

schema.headline: More than 170 migrants rescued after boat catches fire in Channel
